initiatives.title: Locum Compensation Redesign — the 10% and what replaces it
initiatives.why: The 10% deduction taken off every practitioner before their share is the single most resented part of the pay scheme, and it is applied unevenly: one practitioner's orthodontic work is lifted out before the 10% is struck, under a separate agreement made years ago, while another doing the same procedures is charged in full. The owner's direction is to stop deducting it altogether rather than renegotiate the exemption — abolition closes the gap without anyone having to defend why it existed. The question is not whether, it is how it gets funded. A small per-visit charge set by the clinic is the candidate, because it also bills the chair time nobody currently invoices.
initiatives.next: Model the swap properly and take it to the practitioners: drop the 10%, introduce a modest per-visit charge patients are used to paying elsewhere. Then decide the fee level, what happens to existing treatment contracts, and how it is announced.
initiatives.gate: Do not announce the relief before the funding is settled — a benefit given and then partially withdrawn is worse than never given. Also settle what happens to patients mid-treatment, where the per-visit charge lands hardest.
initiatives.timeline: Figures rebuilt in Aug 2026 from the actual monthly workbooks rather than estimates, and independently verified. Direction set by the owner. Fee level, grandfathering and announcement still open; the wording rides on the contractor agreement.

tasks.t: Quantify the two legacy carve-outs (X-ray sharing; the ortho exemption)

Establish what the deduction actually costs and who gains if it goes — read from the real workbooks, not estimated
Confirm the direction: stop deducting rather than renegotiate the one-practitioner exemption

Decide how patients already mid-treatment are handled — the charge falls hardest on the most frequent visitors

Write the whole scheme into the contractor agreement rather than announcing it in a meeting
Announce, with the relief and the funding presented together

initiatives.note: Three things make this work. The relief is progressive — as a share of pay the lowest earners gain most and the highest earner gains least, because most of that practitioner's base was already exempt. So abolition quietly equalises the legacy arrangement without singling anyone out. Second, roughly a third of all visits currently carry no charge at all — orthodontic reviews booked upfront, delivery appointments, and consultations individual practitioners feel unable to bill. A clinic-set charge captures that chair time uniformly without asking anyone to change how they work. Third, this is the first patient charge the clinic controls rather than the practitioners. ⚠️ The relief must be measured on the economic basis (including the founder's computed but undrawn share), not the cash basis — the cash figure is flattered by a subsidy that ends the day she stops working.

initiatives.title: Front-of-House SOP, Training & Bench
initiatives.why: The clinic has no SOP for issuing letters to patients — medical certificates, referral letters, insurance reports, quotations. Nobody had ever said whose job it was, and that gap caused real friction between a doctor and the office. It is a symptom of a bigger one: a whole class of routine patient-facing admin has never been assigned or trained, so it defaults to whoever feels responsible, usually a doctor. The rule should be simple — the doctor supplies the clinical judgement, the front desk produces the document, the message and the follow-through.
initiatives.next: Erincy moves to roughly 70/30 chairside-to-front-desk inside her first three months. The training runs once the new accounting system is ready and now has a fixed scope and attendee list. Letters turn out to need only templates and a short written procedure.
initiatives.gate: Capacity before capability — the desk cannot take on harder work while it is one person deep. Build the bench first, then load it.
initiatives.timeline: Bench building now. One combined training block once the new system is live — covering receipts, the digital form, letters, and handling difficult conversations.

initiatives.title: Locum Invoice Crossover & Payment Date
initiatives.why: Payment used to fall on one date and quietly moved to another, and nobody explained why. The date itself was never the real issue — the cost of moving it back is about sixty ringgit a month. The real issue is that a laboratory cost can arrive after the month has been closed, and there was no agreed rule for which month it then belongs to.
initiatives.next: Decided: the payment date stays where it is, and late invoices carry forward at their original month's rate. Both clauses go to counsel. In parallel, the supplier exercise identifies which suppliers deliver late — that list is the real risk.
initiatives.gate: A laboratory cost belongs to the month the procedure was done, not the month the invoice arrived. A cost carried into a later month is deducted at the share that applied in its original month — and shown separately on the statement.
initiatives.timeline: Decided 29 July. Clauses to counsel next. Full automation becomes possible once the accounting integration and payables onboarding are done.

Before anything can be taken over, we need to know the full universe of who we buy from and how each relationship actually runs today.
initiatives.next: The office has committed to completing the supplier information by the end of August. Reiterated to the lead orthodontist that the intent is to move supplier contact to the practice so clinicians can stay on clinical work.

initiatives.why: Suppliers give us more than goods — early-payment cashback, volume discounts, seasonal promotions, free units, sponsored courses. initiatives.gate: The benefit follows the cost and the risk. Whoever bore the thing that earned the rebate, gets the rebate.

initiatives.note: Cash-flow-earned benefits are the clinic's outright. Case-cost-earned benefits reduce the cost line and reach the doctors automatically — paying them on top would be double-counting. Personal benefits are declared and logged.

initiatives.title: Invisalign Invoice Verification — off the doctor
initiatives.why: A doctor personally checks every aligner invoice to make sure we were billed correctly. The right question is what she is checking it against — and the answer exposes the design flaw: she is reconstructing the truth at month end from knowledge only she holds. Verification belongs with the office, in line with the direction that all supplier communication and invoicing sits with management. The office already has portal access; the obstacle is that the account is segregated by invoice rather than by patient name, so an invoice line cannot be traced back to a case without the doctor's knowledge.
initiatives.next: Folded into the wider supplier exercise rather than run separately — the assessment happens when the supplier list comes back.
initiatives.gate: Capture the truth when it is created, not months later. The doctor confirms the case at the moment it is ordered — thirty seconds — and the office verifies the invoice against that log with no doctor involved.
initiatives.timeline: Access and price list Aug → case log running Sep → first office-run verification Oct. Automated matching later.

tasks.t: Office portal access — already in place
Define exactly what is needed to tie an invoice line to a case, given the account is invoice-segregated not patient-segregated
Obtain the current price list and volume-tier agreement
Start the case log — case ID, patient, doctor, product, date, refinements
First month verified by the office, checked alongside the doctor
Automated invoice-to-case matching to flag discrepancies

initiatives.note: Volume-tier pricing on aligners is a cost-line rebate under the rebates policy.

initiatives.title: AI Clinical Note Transcription
initiatives.why: The clinician wants a readable transcript of her consultations that she can go back over afterwards. That is a transcription problem, not a reasoning one — so it can run entirely on a local machine with no patient audio leaving the building, which removes the privacy objection outright.
initiatives.next: Buy a local transcription tool, record one real consultation and let her read the output. If it is usable, build the speaker-labelling properly. If it is not, no amount of engineering fixes it.
initiatives.gate: Two non-negotiables: patient consent for recording, and the doctor reviews and approves before anything enters the clinical record. Never auto-write.
initiatives.timeline: Test in August. Build the speaker labelling only if the transcript itself passes.

tasks.t: Buy a local transcription app and run one real consultation through it
Have the clinician read the transcript and say whether she can work with it
Test it on a genuinely mixed-language consultation — that is where accuracy falls over
If it passes, add speaker separation so it is clear who said what
Enrol the clinician's voice so her turns are labelled automatically
Agree consent wording and where the recordings are stored
Decide later whether to add local summarising on top of the transcript

initiatives.note: Everything runs offline on an Apple Silicon machine — no data leaves the premises and no external service is involved. Keep summarising out of the first version: a transcript cannot be wrong in the way a summary can. Paired request from the same clinician: pre-visit questionnaires (see the onboarding form initiative) — both serve the same goal, less consultation time on the chair. Architecture direction (10 Aug): wired USB boundary mic per surgery into the existing room PC (no batteries, nothing to charge), audio sent over the clinic network to one central machine that does the transcription, transcript appears in a browser tab on the room PC, session labelled automatically from the appointment book by room and time.

initiatives.title: Patient Conversation Context for Doctors
initiatives.why: When a patient arrives having asked something technical by message beforehand, the doctor needs that context. The agreed short-term fix is to put the messaging app on a surgery computer for the upstairs doctors — recorded here so it gets re-examined rather than quietly becoming permanent.
initiatives.next: Confirm the placement, then decide whether the shared computer is the right long-term answer or an interim.
initiatives.gate: The messaging app is a channel; the patient record is the system of record. Context should reach the doctor where they already look.
initiatives.timeline: Interim placement now. Target state — front desk logs the substance onto the appointment note — lands with the front-of-house SOP.

tasks.t: Confirm placement — the lab space opposite the rooms on each floor, so no doctor is advantaged or disadvantaged
Check the linked-device limit — it cannot go on every doctor's machine
Front desk logs the substance of message exchanges onto the appointment note
Review after a month: is the shared computer still needed?

initiatives.note: A shared computer is a workaround. The real fix is the front-of-house SOP, which puts the context into the record.

initiatives.title: DSA Training Programme
initiatives.why: There is no structured training for the dental surgery assistants and no written standard for how the floor runs during a clinical day. Two doctors have now raised chairside and floor conduct. Most of it looks uninstructed rather than deliberate — nobody has ever written down what good looks like.
initiatives.next: Ask the two senior assistants to build and run a peer-led session, paid, over dinner for the whole team, focused on doctor-specific chairside preferences. Separately, verify the feedback with the general manager and put the conduct standard in writing.
initiatives.gate: A competency matrix per assistant, a quarterly session, and a sign-off — so it feeds the staff scorecard rather than being a one-off.
initiatives.timeline: Verify and write the standard in August. First session once the accounting system training is out of the way.

tasks.t: Ask the two senior assistants to design and run the session, and agree a fee
Verify the feedback with the general manager before anything is said to the team
Check whether the senior-junior pairing is holding in practice, and define what a junior is signed off to do alone
Write the floor and chairside conduct standard and issue it separately from the training night
Book the dinner and run the first session
Draft the competency matrix per assistant
Fold competencies into the staff scorecard

initiatives.note: Keep the training night and the conduct standard apart. The session is a reward and a skills exercise; if the grievances are read out that evening it becomes a reprimand with food. The durable fix is filling the chairs so the idle time does not exist — but that is a six-month lever and the standard is needed now.

initiatives.title: New Doctor — capacity & case-mix hire
initiatives.why: Our own margin data shows a very wide spread in value produced per chair-hour between doctors — one clinician generates several hundred times the true margin per hour of another. Business as usual will not close the gap in time. A clinician who can arrive and immediately deliver higher-value procedures, and bring patients with them, is the case-mix lever — the only route past the capacity ceiling other than extending hours.
initiatives.next: The lead orthodontist conversation is done — she is open to mentoring but was clear that it has to be paid properly. Next: have a draft contract ready for the 17 Aug meeting with the candidate and the general manager, then put the two doctors in a room together to see whether the working relationship fits.
initiatives.gate: Nothing becomes public until the practitioners already here have been heard. Expect the objection that chairs are not full as it is — the honest answer is that retention, not new patient flow, is what separates a full book from an empty one here, and the data supports that.
initiatives.timeline: Contract draft by 16 Aug → candidate meeting 17 Aug → introduction to the lead orthodontist → then the wider doctor briefing.

tasks.t: Text Dr Azelia and Dr Priscilla to book the same one-to-one conversations held with the other doctors
Lead orthodontist approached — open to mentoring, wants fair remuneration
Have a draft contract ready to discuss technically
Meet the candidate and the general manager on 17 August
Decide employee versus contractor, and floor versus recoverable draw, with counsel
Introduce the candidate and the lead orthodontist in person
Settle the mentorship fee with the lead orthodontist
Brief the other doctors before anything is announced

initiatives.note: Shape under discussion is a guaranteed monthly minimum or the calculated fee, whichever is higher, for the first six months. That plus supervision looks a lot like employment, so the engagement basis needs a legal answer before it is offered. Communication to the existing doctors remains the main risk.

initiatives.title: Recall Campaign Expansion — cold blast & post-visit follow-up
initiatives.why: The recall system was built with more triggers than the six, nine and twelve-month recalls we actually switched on. Turning the others on is the cheapest top-line lever available, and the P&L trajectory says business as usual will not close the gap. Messaging even ten thousand lapsed patients costs on the order of RM3,000.
initiatives.next: Decision taken: send from the landline. Brief the vendor, then ship the review ask — it needs only a direct review link and no redirect.
initiatives.gate: Do not launch anything while the recall link is broken — blasting the whole base into a browser security warning is worse than not blasting at all.
initiatives.timeline: UNBLOCKED 18 Jul — the recall link certificate is renewed (valid to 16 Oct) and the vendor has automated the renewal. Post-visit follow-up amendment first (fast, free), then the cold blast.

tasks.t: Decision taken — send from the landline now; stop waiting on the mobile approval
Brief the vendor to send the post-appointment message from the landline
Vendor renewed the expired certificate on the recall link — 18 Jul, valid to 16 Oct
Amend the post-appointment follow-up to also ask for a Google review — no reward, just that it helps others find us
Draft the cold reactivation blast, with a bring-the-family angle
De-conflict against the reactivation call lists so nobody gets both
Send, then measure honestly — correlation is not proven lift
Birthday messages — de-prioritised
Certificate auto-renewal automated by the vendor (cron added, confirmed 21 Jul)

initiatives.note: Birthday trigger de-prioritised by the owner. The review ask moves a lever that already feeds the website automatically.

initiatives.title: Discount Policy & Patient Payment Plans
initiatives.why: Discounting has never had a written rule, so it became a personal judgement call rather than a clinic position. Two years of ledger data show it is concentrated almost entirely in high-value orthodontic case starts settled upfront, and that the clinic quietly carries the larger half of every discount a practitioner gives — because the discount is deducted from the shared base before the split. The practitioner decides; the clinic pays more of it. That is the misalignment to fix. The tool itself is legitimate and stays, but its cost has to be visible to the person holding it.
initiatives.next: Pine Labs meeting confirmed for Tuesday 11 August, 9:30am — bank-agnostic instalment plans. Non-committal rate discovery: merchant rates by instalment tenure, whether the cost can be passed to or shared with the practitioner, settlement timing and any minimum ticket or volume commitment. Separately, the concession clause is now drafted into the contractor agreement.
initiatives.gate: Do not publish or advertise any discount or instalment offer. The dental council's conduct code treats discounts in advertising as an inducement, and bars 'lowest price' style claims. Instalments are offered in the chair, on request, never marketed.
initiatives.timeline: Pine Labs 11 Aug 9:30am. Policy lands inside the contractor agreement rather than as a standalone memo.

tasks.t: Pine Labs Tue 11 Aug 9:30am — question list prepared and sent to Telegram
Confirm June's cases against the practice-management system
Land the concession clause in the contractor agreement — whoever decides a concession carries it
Get counsel's view on the discount under the professional conduct rules on inducement
Separate the trial-appliance pricing from the cash-flow discount before writing policy
Add reason codes so concessions can be told apart in reporting

initiatives.note: June's actual discounts ran 3.7 to 7.2 per cent, below the level at which an instalment plan pays for itself as a straight replacement for discounting. So the instalment product is better aimed at patients who cannot pay upfront — today the clinic finances those itself, interest-free and carrying the risk. The discounting behaviour is structural: practitioners are paid on collections, so pulling payment forward pulls their own pay forward.

initiatives.title: WhatsApp Procedure Shortcuts & Chat Automation
initiatives.gate: All reply wording passes the content truth-gate: no prices, no named dentists, no outcome or reply-time promises.
initiatives.why: The website now opens WhatsApp conversations with a pre-typed, procedure-specific first line (CTA pop-up, live 10 Aug 2026), so incoming chats arrive already labelled by intent: aligners, wisdom tooth, implants, whitening, a child first visit. Today every one of those chats needs a hand-written reply from the front desk, which means answer quality depends on who is on shift and slow replies lose warm leads. A small library of saved quick replies per key procedure (what it is, what a first visit looks like, common questions) lets anyone on the desk send a good first answer in seconds. WhatsApp Business quick replies and greeting or away automations cover most of this without new software.
initiatives.next: Draft delivered 10 Aug: 20 quick replies in 3 tiers at Branding & Marketing/WhatsApp Quick Replies (draft 2026-08-10).md. Shortcut list was derived from 24 months of production data, not assumption: checkup and cleaning touches 82% of patients and is 66% of all first visits, fillings 37%, pain visits 22%, braces only 11% by headcount but the top follow-on (12.4% of cleaning-first new patients convert into it). Only 44% of new patients ever return, so the first-visit reply is the highest-leverage one. Awaiting owner mark-up. Two flags to resolve first: Myobrace was billed 71 times in 24 months but the fact sheet says do not mention it, and there is zero insurance income across 24 months so no draft mentions insurance.
initiatives.note: Chats opening with the pop-up pre-typed lines are pop-up leads; front desk should tag them so click-to-booking attribution stays cheap.

tasks.t: Draft quick-reply library — DONE 10 Aug: 20 replies in 3 tiers, list derived from 24mo production data
Owner sign-off on wording (content truth-gate) + resolve Myobrace & insurance flags
Load as WhatsApp Business quick replies + brief front desk
Greeting / away-hours auto-reply
Front desk tags pop-up-opener chats for attribution

initiatives.timeline: Aug: draft quick-reply library + owner sign-off. Sep: live as WhatsApp Business quick replies, front desk briefed. Oct: greeting/away automations + first attribution review.

drafts.label: T1 · Hours, address & parking
drafts.body:
We're open:
*Mon to Fri* 9.30am to 5.30pm
*Sat* 9.30am to 3.30pm
*Sun & public holidays* closed

We're at 75 & 75A, Jalan SS 22/23, Damansara Jaya, 47400 Petaling Jaya.

There's parking along the road and in the lots behind the shops. We're on the ground floor, so no stairs or lift needed.

Want us to find you a time?

drafts.label: T1 · How to book
drafts.body:
Happy to get you booked in.

Just send us:
1. Patient's full name
2. Contact number
3. Whether you've been to us before
4. Roughly when suits you, morning or afternoon, and which days

If it's for your child, their age helps too.

We'll check the book and come back with the closest times we have.

drafts.label: T1 · First visit — what happens
drafts.body:
Welcome, and thanks for thinking of us.

A first visit is mostly about getting to know you. The dentist will:
• Go through your dental and medical history
• Check your teeth, gums and bite
• Take an x-ray if it's needed to see what's happening below the surface
• Talk you through anything worth keeping an eye on

If something needs attention, the dentist will explain what it is and what the options are before anything is done. Nothing gets started without you agreeing to it.

Most people are with us around an hour for a first visit, though it depends what's found.

Shall we look for a time?

drafts.label: T1 · The "how much" question
drafts.body:
Fair question, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you actually need.

The same treatment can be simple for one person and more involved for another, so quoting a number before the dentist has looked wouldn't be doing you any favours.

What we can promise is no surprises. Once the dentist has assessed you, you'll get the cost explained clearly before any treatment starts, and you decide from there.

We take card, cash, DuitNow QR and bank transfer.

Want to come in for an assessment first?

drafts.label: T1 · In pain, wants to be seen
drafts.body:
Sorry to hear that, let's get you looked at.

So we can prioritise you properly, tell us:
• Where the pain is
• How long it's been going on
• Is it constant, or only when you eat or drink something hot or cold
• Any swelling on the face or gum

If there's facial swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a fever, please treat that as urgent and go to a hospital emergency department rather than waiting for a dental appointment.

Otherwise, send us the above and we'll find you the earliest slot we have.

drafts.label: T1 · Scale & polish
drafts.body:
A scale and polish is the routine clean and check most people come in for.

The dentist or hygienist clears away the hardened plaque that builds up along the gumline, which brushing alone can't shift, then polishes the teeth. You'll also get a check of your teeth, gums and bite while you're in the chair.

Gums can feel a bit tender for a day or so after, especially if it's been a while. That usually settles on its own.

Most people come in around twice a year, but the dentist will suggest what's right for you.

Want us to find you a slot?

drafts.label: T2 · Fillings / decay
drafts.body:
Sounds like it's worth getting looked at.

A filling repairs a tooth where decay or a chip has damaged it. The dentist cleans out the damaged part and rebuilds the tooth with a tooth-coloured material, so it blends in rather than showing up dark.

It's usually done in one visit, and numbing is used so you shouldn't feel the work itself. The tooth can be a little sensitive for a few days afterwards.

If the damage has gone deeper than a filling can handle, the dentist will talk you through the other options before doing anything.

Send us a photo if you like, though we'd still need to see it properly to be sure. Want to come in?

drafts.label: T2 · Tooth extraction
drafts.body:
Taking a tooth out is usually a last resort, so the first step is having the dentist look and see whether it can be saved.

If it does need to come out, the area is numbed first, so you'd feel pressure rather than pain. Afterwards you'll get instructions on eating, rinsing and keeping the area clean while it heals.

Do let us know if you're on any blood thinners or have a heart condition, as the dentist will want to know before the day.

If there's a gap left behind, there are ways to fill it, and the dentist can walk you through those when the time is right.

Want us to find you a time to get it checked?

drafts.label: T2 · Bleeding or sore gums
drafts.body:
Bleeding or sore gums are worth getting checked rather than waiting them out.

Gums often bleed when there's hardened plaque sitting along the gumline, irritating the tissue. A clean can settle that in many cases. If it's gone further, the dentist may recommend a deeper clean below the gumline, sometimes with a bit of numbing to keep you comfortable.

Either way, the dentist will look first and explain what they're seeing before recommending anything.

Bleeding when brushing isn't something to just live with, so it's worth a look. Want to come in?

drafts.label: T2 · Root canal
drafts.body:
Root canal treatment is what's done when the nerve inside a tooth has become infected or damaged, usually from deep decay or a crack.

The idea is to save the tooth rather than lose it. The dentist cleans out the inside of the tooth, disinfects it and seals it up. The area is numbed throughout, so it's generally much more comfortable than its reputation suggests.

It's often done over more than one visit, depending on the tooth. Afterwards the tooth can be more brittle, so the dentist may suggest a crown to protect it.

If you're in pain right now, tell us and we'll prioritise getting you seen.

drafts.label: T2 · Child's first visit
drafts.body:
Lovely, we see plenty of children.

The first visit is mostly about letting them get comfortable. The dentist will count the teeth, have a look at how things are developing, and keep it light. If your child isn't ready for much on the day, that's completely fine, the dentist works at their pace.

It also gives you a chance to ask about brushing, thumb sucking, diet, or anything you've noticed.

It helps if you can tell us their age and anything specific you've spotted, so we can allow the right amount of time.

Shall we find you a slot?

drafts.label: T3 · Braces & clear aligners
drafts.body:
Happy to help you look into it.

There's more than one way to straighten teeth. Fixed braces are the familiar option, and clear aligners are the removable, largely invisible route. We work with Invisalign, Angel Aligner and ClearSmile.

Which one suits you depends on what needs moving and how much, which is why it starts with an assessment. The dentist looks at your teeth, bite and jaw, usually with x-rays or a scan, then talks you through the realistic options and what each involves.

It's an assessment, not a commitment. Plenty of people come in just to find out where they stand.

It helps to know: is this for you or someone else, and roughly what's bothering you about your smile?

drafts.label: T3 · Children's myofunctional
drafts.body:
Glad you asked, this is something we look at closely.

Myofunctional orthodontics is about the habits and muscle patterns behind how a child's jaw and teeth develop: how they breathe, where the tongue rests, whether the lips seal. Things like mouth breathing, snoring or crowded teeth can be signs worth assessing.

An assessment looks at the whole picture, including developmental history, muscle function and airway, alongside the teeth themselves. Depending on what's found, treatment may involve a removable appliance worn mostly at night, plus simple exercises.

It works best while a child is still growing, so it's worth asking early rather than waiting.

Tell us how old your child is and what you've noticed, and we'll take it from there.

drafts.label: T3 · Crowns & bridges
drafts.body:
A crown is a cap that covers a tooth that's too damaged or weak for a filling to hold, protecting what's left and restoring the shape.

A bridge does a similar job across a gap, using the teeth either side for support.

It usually takes more than one visit. The dentist prepares the tooth and takes a mould or scan, then the crown is made and fitted at a later appointment. You're generally given a temporary one in between.

There are different materials, and the dentist will talk through which makes sense for your tooth and where it sits in your mouth.

Want to come in and have it assessed?

drafts.label: T3 · Dentures
drafts.body:
Dentures replace missing teeth and can be a full set or a partial one that fills specific gaps.

It's done over several visits: an assessment first, then moulds, a try-in so you can see how they look and feel before they're finished, and finally fitting. The try-in stage is there so adjustments happen before anything is final.

New dentures do take some getting used to, with eating and speaking, and small adjustments afterwards are normal rather than a sign anything's wrong.

If you're weighing dentures against other ways of replacing teeth, the dentist can go through the comparison with you.

Shall we book you in for a look?

drafts.label: T3 · Dental implants
drafts.body:
An implant replaces a missing tooth from the root up. A small titanium or zirconia post is placed into the jawbone and, once it's integrated, a crown is fitted on top so it works and looks like a normal tooth.

Whether it's suitable depends on the bone in that area and your general health, which is why it starts with an assessment. We use cone beam CT scanning to see the bone in three dimensions and plan properly.

It's not a quick process, as healing time between stages is part of it, and the dentist will map out the timeline for your case.

Want to come in and find out whether it's an option for you?

drafts.label: T3 · Teeth whitening
drafts.body:
We do professional take-home whitening.

The dentist takes a mould so custom trays are made to fit your teeth, then you wear them at home with the gel, following the instructions you're given. Custom trays matter, as they keep the gel on the teeth and off the gums.

A check first is important. Whitening works on natural tooth surface, so existing fillings, crowns or veneers won't change colour, and the dentist will want to make sure your teeth and gums are healthy before starting.

Results vary from person to person, and some people find their teeth are a little sensitive during the process.

Want to come in for a look first?

drafts.label: T3 · Veneers / smile makeover
drafts.body:
Veneers are thin facings bonded to the front of the teeth, used to change shape, colour, spacing or the look of chips.

There's more than one route. Some are built up directly in the chair, others are made in a lab and bonded on afterwards. Which suits you depends on what you'd like to change and the condition of the teeth underneath, and some cases are better served by whitening or straightening first.

It usually involves some preparation of the tooth surface, so it's worth understanding properly before committing. The dentist will go through what's involved and what's realistic for your teeth.

Tell us what you'd like to be different and we'll take it from there.

drafts.label: T3 · Wisdom teeth
drafts.body:
Wisdom teeth are the last ones through, and there often isn't room for them, which is where the trouble starts.

Not every wisdom tooth needs removing. Some sit fine. The ones worth assessing are those causing pain, swelling, repeated gum infections, or pressing on the tooth in front.

The dentist will take an x-ray to see the position and the roots, as that's what determines how straightforward removal would be. If it's more complex, that will be explained, along with the aftercare.

If you're in pain or there's swelling now, say so and we'll get you seen sooner.

Want us to find you a time?

drafts.label: T3 · Night guard / grinding
drafts.body:
Grinding and clenching often happen during sleep, so many people don't realise they're doing it. Signs include a sore jaw in the morning, headaches, sensitive teeth, or a partner mentioning the noise.

Over time it can wear the teeth down, so it's worth getting looked at.

A night guard is a custom-made shield worn while you sleep. It takes the wear instead of your teeth. The dentist takes a mould so it's made to fit you, and you collect it at a second visit.

The dentist will also check how your teeth are meeting and whether anything else is contributing.

Want us to book you in for an assessment?

initiatives.title: Referral Baseline & Early Thank-Yous
initiatives.why: Audited 10 Aug: referral capture stopped in 2014. Of 3,259 referral records in the practice system, 99.8 per cent were created before 2015 — the years since produce single digits, and several produce nothing at all. So referrals may well still be happening; the practice simply stopped recording them. Historically, patient referrals ran about two to one ahead of doctor referrals, which is the channel the referral engine is built on.
initiatives.next: Capture first, reward second. Add the referral question to the intake form and the front-desk script so the field starts filling again. In parallel, keep the NGO conversation moving so the thank-you is ready the day data starts arriving — and use the existing family groupings to build a first thank-you list from data already held.
initiatives.gate: If the system shows no referral data, the front-desk capture question becomes the prerequisite (it is already on the onboarding-form initiative).
initiatives.timeline: Audit done 10 Aug. Capture question live with the intake form work. First thank-you list from family groupings can be built now without waiting for new capture.
